summary:
North Macedonia carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct or for being transgender. Homosexuality was decriminalised in 1996 as a Council of Europe accession condition, and the anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation and gender identity following the 2019 amendments to the Criminal Code, which explicitly list both grounds under the hate speech provisions. The Law on Primary Education adopted in July 2019 likewise introduced anti-discrimination language covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and the 2019 US Country Report found the government enforced such laws in access to government services including health care.

Legal gender recognition remains the central unresolved gap for a trans visitor carrying documents. ILGA-Europe and the ERA LGBTI Enlargement Review 2024, working with the National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia, identify Legal Gender Recognition as the top priority; the government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the LGR chapter a day before Parliamentary Committee review. In January 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that requiring sex reassignment surgery before changing a gender marker violated human rights and awarded €9,000 in damages, but NGOs report the government still fails to recognise gender identity changes in identification documents. A visitor should therefore expect documents to reflect a marker that may not match presentation.

Public trans organising proceeds openly. TransFormA's March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje marked Transgender Day of Visibility on 30 March 2024 under the words "we march bravely", and the first Pride Parade took place in June 2019. A 2025 Pride Parade drew lower attendance after organisers declared it a protest, and foreign embassies pulled funding.

The protective machinery around such events is thin. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious and continuing problem with countless reports and no meaningful state response, a reading the European Commission's country report shares. The 2019 US Country Report deemed the Skopje public prosecutor ineffective in processing hate speech cases and found the LGBTQ community "still prejudiced and harassed by the society, media and the authorities", with hate speech on social media following the June 2019 Pride Parade. In September 2023 the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist with sexual-orientation and gender-identity aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code, one documented instance of the aggravation working in practice.

Violence against LGBTI people is documented and under-reported. The 2019 US Country Report details fellow students verbally and physically attacking a gay high school student, breaking his nose; the student reported the incident to the principal but chose not to report it to police. The same report cites CSO Coalition Margini documenting 70 cases of violence against LGBTI individuals in 2019, including five discrimination cases and one verbal assault by a police officer, and notes most such violence goes unreported to police or institutions. It also states there are many reports about public humiliations, worker firings and even casting homosexual teenagers onto the streets due to revelation of their sexual orientations. Global Voices reported in March 2024 a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

Same-sex relationships carry no recognition. Family law defines marriage as "a union between a man and a woman", and a 2014 government motion sought a constitutional amendment to the same effect, requiring two-thirds of MPs. A 2015 constitutional amendment that would have barred legal recognition of same-sex relations absent a two-thirds majority passed committee 72-4 and was approved in Parliament on 20 January 2015. ECRI has called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries.

Support infrastructure exists in the capital. The LGBTI Support Center in Skopje, a subsidiary of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, offers free legal aid, and EGAL is the oldest organisation working on gay and lesbian health issues.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Europe Index ranked Macedonia worst in the Balkans at −2 on the 17-to−7 scale in February 2012, the only Balkan country in the "red zone" of gross human-rights violations and discrimination. The ranking has since moved with the 2019 legal reforms, but the historical position frames how regional observers read the country.

Strumica Mayor Kostadin Kostadinov nullified all memoranda with LGBTQ organisations in June 2023 and vowed to veto future ones, an instance of sub-national official hostility toward organised LGBTI work. Serbian and North Macedonian LGBTI groups quantified in October 2023 how anti-LGBTQ discrimination harms their economies, casting discrimination as a measurable drag on growth and jobs.

Public opinion has been measured as sharply hostile: polling by the Center for Civil and Human Rights in 2002 found over 80% of respondents viewed homosexuality as "a psychiatric disorder that endangered families" and about 65% considered it a crime warranting jail. North Macedonia ranked 10th worst European country for LGBTQ tourists in 2019.
localsOnly:

Resident-facing support includes the LGBTI Support Center in Skopje, a subsidiary of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, providing free legal aid, and EGAL, the oldest organisation working on gay and lesbian health issues. The National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia works the Legal Gender Recognition file with ILGA-Europe and ERA LGBTI.

Marriage is constitutionally and statutorily restricted to one man and one woman, and the 2015 parliamentary approval of the constitutional amendment on 20 January 2015 entrenched that position. Same-sex relationships remain unrecognised in family law.

Everyday exposure to hostility is recorded: the 2019 US Country Report found the Skopje public prosecutor ineffective in processing hate speech cases, and CSO Coalition Margini documented 70 cases of violence against LGBTI individuals in 2019, with most such violence unreported to police or institutions.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2023 Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentence on aggravating grounds has been appealed or has entered into force is not sourced here. The two-year figure is as reported by ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024.

The current status of the Draft Law on Civil Registry after its withdrawal is unresolved in this inventory; no later reintroduction is sourced.

Post-2019 polling on attitudes toward gender identity specifically, as distinct from sexual orientation, is not sourced. The 2002 Center for Civil and Human Rights figures concern homosexuality.

Whether any sub-national authority besides Strumica has moved against LGBTI organisations since June 2023 is not sourced.
